_meta.author: Reese Reilly
_meta.cultural_source: Hawaiian star and constellation names verified against Bishop Museum Planetarium June 2026 sky map and Nā Inoa Hōkū (Johnson & Mahelona). All names should be confirmed by cultural advisor Professor Kaʻiulani Murphy before public deployment.
_meta.notes: Sky dome X/Y positions are for a 500x500 SVG viewport at 20-21°N latitude, June sky at 10pm HST as baseline. Constellation lines connect stars sharing the same constellationGroup value.

constellationGroups.meaning: The Seven — seven stars pointing to Hōkūpaʻa
constellationGroups.note: The two outer bowl stars point directly to Hōkūpaʻa (Polaris). Multiply that distance by five to find the North Star.

constellationGroups.meaning: The Great Fishhook of Māui — with which Māui fished up the islands
constellationGroups.note: The full curving arc of Scorpius traces the shape of Māui's magical fishhook. The heart is Lehuakona (Antares).

constellationGroups.meaning: Cared for by the Moon — a child of the Moon
constellationGroups.note: The long axis of the cross points to the south celestial pole. Use Kamailemua and Kamailehope (the Pointer Stars) to locate it.

constellationGroups.meaning: The First and Last Maile — two pointer stars leading to the Southern Cross
constellationGroups.note: Draw a line from Kamailehope through Kamailemua and follow it to find Hānaiakamalama (the Southern Cross).

constellationGroups.meaning: Star of the Frigate Bird — kite-shaped constellation surrounding Hōkūleʻa
constellationGroups.note: Hōkūleʻa (Arcturus) is the brightest star in this kite-shaped constellation. The whole shape helps locate the zenith star of Hawaiʻi.

constellationGroups.meaning: The Small Crown — a delicate arc of stars near Hōkūleʻa
constellationGroups.note: A small but distinctive arc of stars just east of Hōkūleʻa. Easy to recognize once you know Boötes.

constellationGroups.meaning: The King — a northern circumpolar constellation
constellationGroups.note: A circumpolar constellation visible year-round from Hawaiʻi. Its distinctive house shape sits near Hōkūpaʻa in the northern sky.

constellationGroups.meaning: Voice of Joy (Marquesan name) — the compact southern crow
constellationGroups.note: A compact four-star trapezoid shape in the southern sky. Marquesan name Meʻe — a reminder that Hawaiian navigation knowledge spans the whole Pacific.

constellationGroups.meaning: Named for Keoe — the constellation surrounding Vega
constellationGroups.note: The small parallelogram of stars surrounding brilliant Keoe (Vega). Vega is the anchor of the Ka Lupe o Kāwelo star line.

constellationGroups.meaning: Named for Humu — the triggerfish constellation surrounding Altair
constellationGroups.note: Humu (Altair) is the brightest star in Aquila. The constellation shape resembles a bird in flight across the summer Milky Way.

constellationGroups.meaning: Named for Pīmoe — the great southern constellation
constellationGroups.note: Pīmoe (Sagittarius) marks the direction of the galactic center. The Milky Way is brightest and most spectacular in this direction.

stars.meaning: Star of Joy — zenith star of Hawaiʻi at 21°N
stars.navRole: Tahitian navigators sailed north following Hōkūleʻa to reach Hawaiʻi. It passes directly overhead at 21°N — the latitude of the islands. The voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa is named for it. When Hōkūleʻa is at zenith, you are at the latitude of Hawaiʻi.
stars.obsNote: Tracked by UH 2.2m and Keck; spectral data in IRTF Maunakea archives.

stars.meaning: Stationary Star — the unmoving anchor of the northern sky
stars.riseHouse: Circumpolar — never sets at Hawaiʻi latitude
stars.navRole: The North Star. Its altitude above the horizon equals your latitude — at Hawaiʻi it sits about 20° up. Kept astern when sailing south to Tahiti. When it disappears below the horizon, you have crossed the equator — switch to Hānaiakamalama (the Southern Cross).
stars.obsNote: Used as a calibration reference star for Maunakea telescope pointing systems.

stars.meaning: Glowing / Burning — the brightest star in the Hawaiian sky
stars.navRole: Brightest star in the Hawaiian sky. Passes directly over the latitude of Tahiti (17°S) — used to navigate the return voyage south. Part of the Ke Kā o Makaliʻi star line. Its heliacal rising signals the beginning of the fishing season.
stars.obsNote: One of the nearest stars to Earth. Extensively studied at Keck for stellar atmosphere properties.

stars.meaning: Eyes of the Chief — marks the start of Makahiki, the Hawaiian New Year
stars.spec: Open cluster — approximately 1000 stars, predominantly B-type
stars.navRole: Rising of Makaliʻi at sunset marks Makahiki — the Hawaiian New Year. Gives its name to the star line Ke Kā o Makaliʻi. Also used as a latitude check — its altitude shifts predictably as you sail north or south.
stars.obsNote: Extensively imaged by Subaru Telescope on Maunakea. Part of UKIRT infrared surveys.

stars.meaning: The Great Fishhook of Māui — with which Māui fished up the Hawaiian Islands
stars.spec: M1 Iab+ Red Supergiant (Antares/Lehuakona at center)
stars.navRole: The entire constellation traces the shape of Māui's fishhook. When the hook is at its highest in the south, the navigator knows true south. The heart — Lehuakona (Antares) — confirms the bearing. Dominant sky feature of the Kau dry season.
stars.obsNote: Antares monitored by Keck for stellar mass loss. UKIRT infrared tracks dust shells around this supergiant.

stars.meaning: Southern Lehua Blossom — the red heart of the Fishhook
stars.navRole: The red heart of Kamakaunuiamāui. Its deep red color — visible to the naked eye — made it culturally significant across Polynesia. At its highest point south it confirms true south bearing. Mars occasionally passes close to Lehuakona — navigators were careful not to confuse the two.
stars.obsNote: If placed at the center of our solar system, Antares would extend beyond the orbit of Mars. Monitored at Keck for stellar mass loss.

stars.meaning: Blossom — flowering before the great Dog Star rises
stars.navRole: Part of the Ke Kā o Makaliʻi arc. Rises before Sirius and helps track the curvature of this key star group across the sky.
stars.obsNote: High-resolution spectroscopy conducted at Keck I, Maunakea.

stars.meaning: Cared for by the Moon — a child of the Moon
stars.navRole: Takes over from Hōkūpaʻa once the navigator crosses the equator. The long axis of the cross points to the south celestial pole. Ka Iwikuamoʻo star line runs from Hōkūpaʻa all the way south to Hānaiakamalama.
stars.obsNote: Low elevation from Maunakea. CFHT archive includes Crux region southern sky surveys.

stars.meaning: Star Wreath — northernmost star of the Makaliʻi arc
stars.navRole: Northernmost star of the Ke Kā o Makaliʻi arc. Helps the navigator track the full curvature of this key star line from north to south across the winter sky.
stars.obsNote: Binary star resolved with Keck interferometry at Maunakea.

stars.meaning: Keoe — anchor of the Lyra constellation and Ka Lupe o Kāwelo star line
stars.navRole: Anchor of the Ka Lupe o Kāwelo star line. Rises nearly due northeast and sets nearly due northwest — an excellent compass reference. One of the brightest stars in the summer sky.
stars.obsNote: Vega was the first star other than the Sun to be photographed. Studied at Keck for debris disk structure.

stars.meaning: The Triggerfish — swift-rising equatorial star
stars.navRole: Rises almost exactly due east and sets almost exactly due west — one of the most reliable compass stars for east-west bearings. Part of the summer triangle alongside Keoe (Vega) and Piraʻetea (Deneb).
stars.obsNote: Altair rotates so rapidly it is visibly flattened at its poles — one of very few stars whose surface has been directly imaged.

stars.meaning: Piraʻetea — Tahitian name used across Polynesian navigation tradition
stars.navRole: Third point of the summer triangle with Keoe and Humu. Bishop Museum uses the Tahitian name Piraʻetea — a reminder that navigation knowledge was shared across the whole Pacific triangle of Hawaiʻi, Tahiti, and Aotearoa.
stars.obsNote: Despite being thousands of light years away, Deneb shines brightly because it is one of the most luminous stars known. Studied at Keck for its powerful stellar wind.

stars.meaning: Looking Forward — the forward-facing twin
stars.spec: A1 V + A2 Vm Sextuple System
stars.navRole: Part of the Ke Kā o Makaliʻi arc. Rises just slightly north of its twin Nānāhope (Pollux). Together they bracket a section of the arc. Castor is actually a sextuple star system — six stars bound together.
stars.obsNote: Castor's six-star system has been resolved by interferometry. Studied at CFHT on Maunakea.

stars.meaning: Looking Behind — the rearward-facing twin
stars.navRole: The brighter of the Gemini twins. Part of the Ke Kā o Makaliʻi arc between Capella and Procyon. Helps the navigator track the curvature of this critical winter star line.
stars.obsNote: The nearest giant star to our solar system. It hosts a confirmed exoplanet — Pollux b.

stars.meaning: Hikianalia — a navigation guide star of great importance
stars.spec: B1 III-IV + B2 V Binary (Blue Giants)
stars.navRole: Zenith star for the Marquesas Islands — when Hikianalia is directly overhead, you are at the latitude of the Marquesas, the likely origin point of the Hawaiian migration. The voyaging canoe Hikianalia, sailing partner to Hōkūleʻa, is named for this star.
stars.obsNote: A close binary — the two blue giants orbit each other every four days, distorting each other into egg shapes. Studied at Keck.

stars.meaning: Voice of Joy — Marquesan name for the compact southern crow constellation
stars.navRole: A compact, distinctive southern constellation used as a pointer toward Hikianalia (Spica). Its Marquesan name Meʻe reflects the pan-Pacific knowledge network that Hawaiian navigation belongs to.
stars.obsNote: Corvus region studied for background galaxy surveys using CFHT wide-field imaging at Maunakea.

stars.meaning: Ikiiki — the bright heart of the Lion constellation
stars.navRole: The brightest star in the Leo region of the sky. Rises roughly northeast and sets roughly northwest, useful for east-west compass bearings in the spring sky. Sits on the ecliptic — the path the Sun, Moon, and planets follow — so planets are often found near Ikiiki.
stars.obsNote: Regulus is one of the four Royal Stars of ancient Persian astronomy. Studied at Keck for its rapid rotation.

stars.meaning: The King — a circumpolar northern constellation
stars.navRole: A circumpolar constellation visible year-round from Hawaiʻi. Its distinctive house or crown shape sits near Hōkūpaʻa in the northern sky. Because it never sets, Ka Mōʻī is always available as a northern reference in any season.
stars.obsNote: Delta Cephei in this constellation is the prototype of Cepheid variable stars — the standard candles used to measure cosmic distances. Studied extensively at Maunakea.

stars.meaning: The Last Maile — trailing pointer star to the Southern Cross
stars.spec: G2 V + K1 V Binary (Sun-like stars)
stars.navRole: The nearest star system to our Sun. Together with Kamailemua (Beta Centauri) it forms the two Pointer Stars that indicate Hānaiakamalama (the Southern Cross). Draw a line from Kamailehope through Kamailemua to find the Cross.
stars.obsNote: The nearest star system to Earth at 4.37 light years. Proxima Centauri — its third companion — is even closer at 4.24 light years and hosts a candidate exoplanet.

stars.meaning: The First Maile — leading pointer star to the Southern Cross
stars.navRole: The leading Pointer Star. Together with Kamailehope, it points directly to Hānaiakamalama. The pair are called the Maile Twins — maile being the sacred vine used in Hawaiian ceremony. Finding these two stars and following their line is how the southern navigator locates the south celestial pole.
stars.obsNote: Beta Centauri is actually a triple star system. One of the brightest stars in the southern sky. Studied at CTIO and referenced in Maunakea southern sky calibration.

stars.meaning: The Seven — seven stars that point to Hōkūpaʻa
stars.spec: Asterism — multiple stellar types across Ursa Major
stars.setHouse: Circumpolar — never fully sets from Hawaiʻi
stars.navRole: The two outer stars of the Dipper bowl — called the Pointer Stars — point directly to Hōkūpaʻa (Polaris). Multiply the distance between them by five to find the North Star. Nāhiku is circumpolar from Hawaiʻi and can be used any clear night of the year.
stars.obsNote: Several Big Dipper stars are part of the Ursa Major Moving Group — a cluster of stars born together. Studied at UH 2.2m telescope.

stars.meaning: The Mouth of the Southern Fish — lone bright star of the southern autumn sky
stars.navRole: One of the few bright stars in the southern autumn sky, making it a critical latitude reference when sailing south. Its low position on the southern horizon from Hawaiʻi means its visibility is directly tied to sky darkness — a meaningful dark sky benchmark star for this app.
stars.obsNote: Fomalhaut hosts one of the most photographed debris disks in astronomy — imaged by Hubble and studied at Maunakea for exoplanet candidates.

stars.meaning: Fine Braided Cord — second brightest star in the sky
stars.navRole: Second brightest star in the entire sky. Barely visible from Hawaiʻi — it skims the southern horizon. Its altitude above the horizon tells the navigator precisely how far south of Hawaiʻi they have sailed. When Miloliʻi is high in the sky you are in the southern latitudes near Tahiti.
stars.obsNote: Canopus is used as a navigation reference star by spacecraft including the Voyager probes. Also used for Maunakea telescope attitude calibration.

altNames.name: The Star That Steers the Canoe

stars.meaning: The Star That Steers the Canoe — the dawn and dusk navigator
stars.spec: Planet — brightest object in sky after Sun and Moon
stars.riseHouse: Varies — rises and sets within 3 hours of the Sun
stars.navRole: The most important planet for Polynesian navigation. Appears as the brilliant Evening Star in the west after sunset or as the Morning Star in the east before dawn — providing a precise bearing at the two most critical navigation moments of the day. Never strays far from the Sun's path.
stars.obsNote: Venus is the brightest natural object in the night sky after the Moon. Pioneer Venus and Magellan spacecraft data archived and studied at IfA Hawaiʻi.

stars.meaning: The Strong One — brightest of the wandering stars
stars.spec: Planet — gas giant, brightest true planet
stars.navRole: The brightest true star-like object in the night sky after Venus. Moves slowly enough against the background stars to be used as a temporary compass reference for weeks at a time. Its position relative to fixed stars confirmed latitude and season.
stars.obsNote: Jupiter and its moons extensively studied at Keck Observatory. The Great Red Spot storm is monitored for long-term changes.

stars.meaning: The Red Star — the wandering fire star
stars.spec: Planet — red from iron oxide surface
stars.navRole: Its unmistakable red-orange color — similar to Lehuakona (Antares) — made Mars culturally significant. Navigators were careful not to confuse Mars with Lehuakona when Mars passed near the Scorpius region. This near-conjunction was a notable celestial event.
stars.obsNote: Mars surface features studied using Maunakea telescopes during opposition. The IRTF on Maunakea specializes in Mars atmospheric observations.

stars.meaning: The Slow One — the patient wanderer
stars.navRole: The slowest-moving visible planet — 29 years to complete one circuit. This slow steady movement made it a reliable long-term seasonal marker. A navigator who knew where Kaʻuopae was at voyage start could use its position to track the passage of time over weeks.
stars.obsNote: Saturn's rings and moons studied extensively at Keck. The Cassini spacecraft mission was planned in part using Maunakea observations.

altNames.name: The Long Coral Reef in the Sky

stars.meaning: The Long Coral Reef in the Sky — the great river of stars
stars.navRole: The Milky Way arch itself served as a navigation reference — its orientation changes predictably through the night and seasons. When the galactic center rises in the southeast the navigator knows the summer sky orientation. The dark skies of Maunakea are essential for seeing Koʻa Loa in its full glory.
stars.obsNote: Subaru Telescope wide-field surveys are mapping billions of Milky Way stars. The galactic center is one of Maunakea's primary research targets.

stars.w: Star Line: Capella → Pleiades → Pollux → Procyon → Sirius
stars.meaning: The Canoe-Bailer of Makaliʻi — the great winter navigation arc
stars.navRole: The primary winter star line. The arc runs from Hōkūleī (Capella) in the north through Makaliʻi (Pleiades), Nānāmua and Nānāhope (the Gemini twins), Puana (Procyon), and down to Aʻā (Sirius). This line sweeps across the sky like a giant canoe bailer. Dominant from November through March.
stars.obsNote: Central to Nainoa Thompson's revival of Hawaiian navigation in the 1970s-80s, developed in consultation at the Bishop Museum Planetarium.

stars.w: Star Line: Polaris → Big Dipper → Arcturus → Southern Cross
stars.meaning: The Backbone — the great north-south spine of the sky
stars.riseHouse: North to South — spans the full sky
stars.navRole: The great north-south axis of Hawaiian navigation. Runs from Hōkūpaʻa (Polaris) in the north through Nāhiku (Big Dipper), down through Hōkūleʻa (Arcturus) at zenith, and all the way south to Hānaiakamalama (Southern Cross). A navigator who can see this full line knows their exact orientation.
stars.obsNote: This star line spans the entire visible sky from north to south — a remarkable feat of systematic observation requiring many voyages to fully map.

stars.w: Star Line: Vega → Altair → Spica → Corvus
stars.meaning: The Kite of Kāwelo — the great spring and summer star line
stars.navRole: The spring and summer star line. Runs from Keoe (Vega) in the north through Humu (Altair) and down to Hikianalia (Spica) and Meʻe (Corvus) in the south. Used when Ke Kā o Makaliʻi has set — the seasonal transition between these two lines tells the navigator which half of the year they are in.
stars.obsNote: One of the four Nā Lālani Hōkū — together these four star lines provide navigational reference through all seasons and all hours of the night.

stars.w: Star Line: Scorpius arc through the southern sky
stars.meaning: The Fishhook from Heaven — the great southern star line
stars.navRole: The great southern star line following the arc of Kamakaunuiamāui (Scorpius) across the sky. Dominant in summer when Ke Kā o Makaliʻi is absent. The curving shape mirrors the fishhook of Māui — the navigator reads the whole arc to maintain bearing across the southern ocean.
stars.obsNote: Together with Ke Kā o Makaliʻi, Ka Iwikuamoʻo, and Ka Lupe o Kāwelo, Manaiakalani completes the four Nā Lālani Hōkū providing continuous sky coverage through every season.
